claims.text: The starting material is equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr.
Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr has approximately 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr has a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr undergoes pesting and rapid oxidation under conditions similar to 800 °C in air for 5 hours.
Atomic layer deposition can produce a thin, uniform, adherent Al2O3 coating on as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
An Al2O3 coating will improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr.
A continuous external alumina scale can serve as a barrier that decreases inward oxygen transport.
The alumina scale will be self-healing.
Al2O3 is sufficiently stable at high temperature to constitute a stable external oxide layer.
Restricting oxygen penetration with an alumina barrier will minimize internal oxidation and pesting.
A surface alumina coating will leave the bulk alloy's mechanical integrity largely unaffected.
The coated alloy will exhibit significantly less oxidation and pesting than the untreated alloy during a 5-hour exposure to air at 800 °C.
After coating and oxidation exposure, the alloy will retain its characteristic room-temperature tensile ductility.
After coating and oxidation exposure, the alloy will retain its high-temperature yield strength near 1000 °C at strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1.
The intervention is applicable near 800 °C in air for exposure durations up to 5 hours.
Coating effectiveness and preservation of mechanical behavior depend on coating thickness, adhesion, and integrity during thermal exposure.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls the alumina scale self-healing, whereas cited record PMC7040784::web::004::1_introduction states that crystalline alumina has virtually no fluidity and instead attributes crack-healing behavior to amorphous silica or fluid glass-forming oxides.
